name: fruit
summary: The skin of something grown and picked: an apple. Waxy, taut over a curve, and shinier than anything else alive in this library.
why: A new material rather than a reach for an existing one, and the test this library uses is
whether the surface differs rather than whether the object does. Nothing here is a soft
waxy organic skin. The two nearest are both wrong in a way that shows: skin at 0.78 is
flesh, which scatters and barely returns a highlight, and an apple that rough comes out
as a red potato; ceramic at 0.30 is a fired glaze, which is glass, and an apple that
smooth comes out as a painted bauble.
Roughness 0.42, between the two and nearer the glaze. An apple's wax does return a real
highlight - it is the thing you polish one on a sleeve to get - but it is a soft one
spread over a curve rather than the hard point a glaze gives. Judged against MU's own
art, which is the argument that settles it: apple.OZJ already has a white specular
painted across its top third, so the sheet is telling us the artist saw a shine there.
The material's job is to agree with that painting under a moving light rather than to
add a second one beside it.
Metallic 0.0. It is a dielectric with a strong specular, which is ceramic's trap and
water's: reaching for metallic to get the shine gives an apple cast in copper.
No grain, and for the reason skin gives. A real apple has lenticels and a faint dimple
at the calyx, and the temptation to put a noise field there is real - but the sheet is
sixteen pixels square across the whole fruit, so a lenticel is far below a texel and any
grain would be invented rather than resolved. Fifty triangles of geometry already carry
the only shape there is evidence for.
It is on the apple's body alone. The leaf and stem are two triangles of cut-out card off
pot3, and those are foliage - a different surface on the same object, which is exactly
the split the island assignment exists to make.
